items.stem: Which task is the best candidate for automation?

options.text: A rare one-off task that changes every time
options.rationale: Low volume and high variability make automation poor value.

options.text: A high-volume, repetitive task with consistent steps
options.rationale: Correct: repetitive, stable tasks give the best automation return.

options.text: A task requiring sensitive human judgement each time
options.rationale: Judgement-heavy tasks are poor automation candidates.

options.text: A task no one understands or has mapped
options.rationale: Unmapped, broken processes should be fixed first.

items.explanation: Correct: high-volume, rule-based, repetitive tasks with stable inputs automate best.

items.stem: Which TWO belong in a safe automation's governance? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Access controls on who can edit the automation
options.rationale: Correct: access control limits unsafe changes.

options.text: A cost or usage limit with alerts
options.rationale: Correct: cost limits prevent runaway spend.

options.text: Removing all logging to save storage
options.rationale: Logging is needed to monitor and debug.

options.text: Letting anyone change production flows freely
options.rationale: Unrestricted changes are a governance risk.

items.explanation: Correct: access controls and cost limits are core governance safeguards.

items.stem: An automation step sometimes fails because an external API times out. What is the best design response?

options.text: Add retries with backoff and a fallback path
options.rationale: Correct: this handles transient failures gracefully.

options.text: Assume the API never fails and ignore it
options.rationale: Ignoring failures makes the automation fragile.

options.text: Delete the step so it cannot fail
options.rationale: Removing needed functionality is not a fix.

options.text: Run the whole flow again from scratch every time
options.rationale: Full restarts are wasteful and may duplicate work.

items.explanation: Correct: add retries with backoff and a fallback so a transient failure does not break the whole flow.
